content.title: Reviewer #4
content.review:
I have read the main text as well as the appendix to validate the proofs and check the additional experimental results. 

Summary:

•	The paper proposes a modification to first and second moment updates of ADAM and LAProp, namely MADAM and LAMADAM, such that instead of computing a uniform running average of gradients and their squares, a weighted average is computed. Specifically, instead of $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$, a single parameter $\beta_{t,i}$ for both moment estimations across each coordinate. $\beta_{t,i}$ is chosen to maximize the variance estimate, $v_t,i$, along each individual coordinate. 

•	The paper claims to achieve a rate of $\mathbb E \lVert \nabla f (\theta_a) \rVert^2 = \mathcal O (\log(T) / T)$, where $\theta_a$ is randomly chosen over all iterations.

•	To demonstrate the numerical performance of their algorithms, the authors provide extensive experimental results in comparison with SGD and other adaptive methods for image classification, machine translation and natural language understanding tasks.


Strengths:

•	The paper identifies practical shortcomings of adaptive gradient methods for different regimes of stochastic gradient behavior and proposes a new methodology that could yield improved performance for various tasks.

•	I think the authors motivate their adaptive learning rate in a detailed manner fashion. They provide intuitive explanations as to how the adaptive learning rate behaves with respect to the magnitude of deviation of stochastic gradients from the running average. In section 4, they argue about the convergence properties of their algorithms based on a simple 2-dimensional quadratic problem by presenting iterate trajectories and error values of Adam and MAdam.

•	The paper offers comprehensive experimental evaluation for different tasks under well-known setups. Authors give different perspectives to performance and behavior of their methods in comparison with widely-used optimizers.


Weaknesses:

•	In equation (18) in the appendix, on the second equality, the authors write that $ \mathbb E_t \left[ \frac{g_{t,i}}{\sqrt{ \beta_{t,i} v_{t-1, i} } + \epsilon} | \theta_t \right] =  \frac{ [ f( \theta_t ) ]i }{\sqrt{ \beta_{t,i} v_{t-1, i} } + \epsilon} $. However, computation of $\beta_{t,i}$ depends on $g_{t,i}$ which makes expressions in the numerator and the denominator dependent random variables. One solution might be using lower/upper bound of $\beta_{t,i}$ and only deal with the expected value of $g_{t,i}$. However, we do not know whether the expression inside the expectation $\mathbb E_t \left[ \frac{g_{t,i}}{ \sqrt{ \beta_{t,i} v_{t-1, i} } + \epsilon } | \theta_t \right]$ is positive or negative. This keeps us from picking the appropriate bound on $\beta_{t,i}$. If I am not mistaken in my observation, this equality shouldn’t be valid, which creates a critical problem for the correctness of the theoretical analysis.

•	Regarding the practical performance, the proposed methods have comparable, sometimes better, performance in most tasks. Although the proposed methods show consistent performance across tasks of different nature, their improvements over other optimizers are not very significant. Comparison against SGD for Transformers might have been important to show instability of SGD for such tasks.


Additional Comments:

•	$\mathbb E_t$ is missing in the first 2 lines of Eq. (21) for the summation with coefficient $\eta_t G / 2$. For the same expression, you take $\sqrt{ 1 - \beta_{t,i} }$ outside of both expectation and summation, which shouldn’t be valid. You could lower-bound $\beta_{t,i} \geq \underline{\beta}$, then you could take the expression out.

•	In expression (25), the factor in front of the parenthesis is missing a $G$. It should be $2 \sqrt{\overline{\beta}} G + \epsilon$.


Score:

I vote for clear rejection of this paper, mainly because I suspected there is a mistake in the proof of Theorem 1 as I indicated above in my comments. In my opinion, this paper is rather practically-oriented in the way that it highlights practical performance over theoretical properties. Experiments are extensive and I appreciate the effort that is put into them very much. However, I am also not totally convinced that MADAM and LAMADAM have significantly better performance than other optimizers. I am open for further discussion with the authors about my comments/concerns and their possible future updates/improvements.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Thank you for the careful review!

content.title: Thank you for the careful review!
content.comment:
We really appreciate your careful review! We are also glad that you acknowledge our efforts in explaining the motivation and the extent of experiments we have conducted. Yes there was an error in the original proof for Eq. 18. We have fixed that along with other typos you have pointed out, but with the current proof technique where we only consider the worst-case $\beta_t$ in each step, we reached a worse convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{t})$. Please refer to the updated version for details. We also polished and moved one of the synthetic experiments from the appendix into the main paper (Sec. 4.1), which shows MAdam achieves better empirical and theoretical [1] convergence rate than AMSGrad on this problem. 

We admit that our proof technique is very basic, but our focus is to propose a novel approach to compute the adaptive step sizes and demonstrate its good empirical results, and the proof just shows it does converge. Note the increasing batch size assumption holds in our large-batch experiments, where the smallest batch size (32K) is larger than total number of iterations (2075).

Regarding the practical performance, we have performed thorough hyperparameter search for all the baseline methods on a variety of problems. Our results show consistent improvements on NLP tasks, and the improvement in convergence speed and test scores in the large-batch setting is significant. Our main focus is on improving the training of Transformers, and we do not want to exaggerate its effectiveness for other tasks . For training ResNets on image datasets, we have chosen the best learning rate and learning rate schedules to find the best for the evaluated algorithms. We do not always outperform SGD,  but it is a known issue that AdaGrad or Adam do not outperform SGD when training ResNets on image classification, as shown by the comprehensive studies of Choi et al. [2] and Agarwal et al. [3]. Some existing literatures on improving Adam do not provide convincing experimental setups on image classification to find the best results of SGD to highlight their improvements,  but they are still well accepted, e.g., we have verified that SGD outperforms AdaBound [4] easily if the multi-step learning rate schedule decays the learning rate twice, AdaBelief [5] follows the same schedule as AdaBound on CIFAR, and our results outperforms both papers on CIFAR and ImageNet.


[1] Xiangyi Chen, Sijia Liu, Ruoyu Sun, and Mingyi Hong. On the convergence of a class of Adam-type algorithms for non-convex optimization. ICLR, 2019. 

[2] Choi, Dami, Christopher J. Shallue, Zachary Nado, Jaehoon Lee, Chris J. Maddison, and George E. Dahl. "On empirical comparisons of optimizers for deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.05446 (2019).

[3] Agarwal, Naman, Rohan Anil, Elad Hazan, Tomer Koren, and Cyril Zhang. "Disentangling Adaptive Gradient Methods from Learning Rates." arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.11803 (2020).

[4] Luo, Liangchen, Yuanhao Xiong, Yan Liu, and Xu Sun. "Adaptive gradient methods with dynamic bound of learning rate." ICLR (2019).

[5] Zhuang, Juntang, Tommy Tang, Yifan Ding, Sekhar C. Tatikonda, Nicha Dvornek, Xenophon Papademetris, and James Duncan. "AdaBelief Optimizer: Adapting Stepsizes by the Belief in Observed Gradients." NeurIPS (2020).

content.title: Thank you for your response
content.comment:
**Regarding the practical performance of your method**

-	I agree with you on the fact that LAMADAM shows consistently better performance for NLP tasks. Especially in Table 3 in the updated version, this is verified across different experiments. Although I acknowledge the fact that the performance is consistent across different setups, I am not sure if this is a significant-enough improvement from my point of view. 
-	For the image classification task, your methods is still performing consistently, but I don’t think there is a noticeable improvement, which the authors also agree as far as I understood from their comment.
-	As I mentioned earlier, I appreciate the motivation you provide for your proposed approach and that you try to verify your arguments through simulations, as well. 

**Regarding the theoretical results**

-	If we look at the total complexity of your algorithm, it is obviously worse than the results of Zaheer et al., 2018; the total number of stochastic gradient evaluations are of the same order as theirs due to your linearly-increasing batch size, but your iterate complexity is worse.
-	This paper focuses mainly on practical performance of the proposed method and the convergence result is a justification that the method is convergent. However, in my opinion, having a worse total complexity is still a small downside.

I am open for further exchange of comments to make sure we understand each other’s perspective.

display_title: Interesting idea but the execution of the idea and results aren't sufficient for ICLR

content.title: Interesting idea but the execution of the idea and results aren't sufficient for ICLR
content.review:
This paper proposes a new adaptive algorithm for nonconvex optimization. The distinct feature of the algorithm is to use an iteration dependent second order momentum parameter $\beta_t$, compared to standard constant $\beta$, like ADAM. The authors analyze the convergence of the algorithm for smooth nonconvex optimization and show that with increasing mini-batch sizes, growing as $t+1$, the method has $1/T$ rate and $\epsilon^{-2}$ complexity for squared gradient norm. The authors show that the method has competitive performance in different applications with neural networks.

Pros: General idea of using $\beta_t$ depending on the estimated gradient variance is intuitive and interesting, the explanation of the idea is clear. Moreover, the practical evaluation part is extensive with diverse set of applications.

Concerns: Even though the intuitive role of the choice of $\beta_t$ is well-explained, I think the discussion is kind of vague. I would prefer to see either fully rigorous theoretical justification or some simple empirical evidence (toy experiments just to illustrate the effect) justifying the claims made regarding $\beta_t$. For example, the paragraph after eq (9) can be much clearer if this effects is illustrated with simple experiments.

In addition, the theoretical analysis is quite rough: only the upper and lower bounds of $\beta_t$, which are $\underline \beta$ and $\bar \beta$ are used. The specific form of $\beta_t$ isn't really utilized in the proof, so it isn't clear if the choice of $\beta_t$ brings any benefit in theory. Actually it seems to me the proof would work with any upper and lower bounded $\beta_t$, is this correct?

The proof of Thm 1 follows Zaheer et al,. 2018 and uses increasing batch sizes (b_t = t+1). However, the result of Zaheer et al., 2018 shows that with increasing mini-batch sizes, Adam also works, whereas Adam fails when one uses a single sample (or constant mini-batch size). Therefore, I think that the setting that the authors analyze is too benign: even a non-convergent method (Adam) works with very large mini-batch sizes, therefore the new method converging in this setting doesn't give a complete story. I would suggest to include a more refined analysis using one gradient every iteration like Chen et al., 2019.

In page 4, it is written that "we analyze the case $\alpha=0$, but the analysis should extend to general case". I don't agree with this remark. We know for adaptive methods first order momentum parameter can introduce difficulties  in analysis. For example, Sec 4.3 of [1]. Since the authors use nonzero $\alpha$ in the experiments, I think they should analyze this case.

Even though the experiments are extensive, the performance of the new methods isn't very promising. The method performs almost the same as the existing methods and some methods such as Adagrad and AdamNC are omitted. It seems Amsgrad is also omitted even though the sentence "We also find AMSGRAD improves ..." in Sect 5.1 is unclear. Does the authors mean applying Amsgrad to all the adaptive methods? In that case, what does it mean to apply Amsgrad to other methods? Amsgrad is a distinct optimizer itself.

Minor comment:
Paragraph after eq. (10), why does bounded gradients imply smoothness of $f(\theta)$, or do the authors want to say (10) implies smoothness of $f(\theta)$? 

Overall, even though I find the idea of maximum variance weighted averaging for squared gradients interesting, the execution of the idea doesn't seem sufficient for a top conference. In particular, the theoretical justification for the new $\beta_t$ is missing and the theoretical analysis is loose (not using the specific form of $\beta_t$) without new insights. Moreover, the setting in which the analysis is done is not representative for adaptive methods. Lastly, the empirical merit is unclear. Therefore I vote for a rejection.

[1] Chen, Liu, Xu, Li, Lin, Hong, Cox, ZO-AdaMM: Zeroth-Order Adaptive Momentum Method for Black-Box Optimization, NeurIPs 2019.



=============== after discussion phase ================

I thank the authors for their response. Unfortunately, I am still not convinced about the theoretical results. Analyzing the algorithm in large-batch regime is not very insightful as large (increasing) batch sizes basically makes the algorithm behave like a deterministic method. Moreover, with the mistake that Reviewer 4 identified, the theoretical results of the paper got even worse. The new algorithms behave worse than Adam in the worst-case large-batch case, which contradicts the motivation. Even though the algorithm looks promising in practice, I believe a clear principled reason is necessary to verify the practical observations. Therefore, I keep my score for rejection.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for the time spent reviewing our paper and your great suggestions for further studies. We are glad that you find our idea of the adaptive $\beta_t$ interesting and our empirical evaluations extensive. Although improving our theoretical analysis as you suggested is on top of our list for the future, we believe our empirical analysis already demonstrates its effectiveness. The proposed adaptive running average improves consistently in NLP tasks, and accelerates the convergence of Adam significantly in the large batch setting. We can understand your high standards for the theoretical analysis, which is certainly the selling point of many good papers such as ZO-AdaMM, but unlike the ZO-AdaMM algorithm, which looks almost the same to the original AMSGrad but provides very rigorous theoretical analysis, our greatest contribution is to propose a novel adaptive learning rate and therefore a more distinct algorithm from Adam, which has been shown to be effective on a range of toy and practical datasets.

We apologize for the previous erroneous version of the paper. We have revised the paper to correct the typos, such as the bounded gradient issue you mentioned. We have deleted the remark that "the analysis extends to general case". We have also moved and polished one toy experiment from the appendix to the main paper (now Sec 4.1). This toy experiment comes from another paper of Chen et al. [1], where we show MAdam achieves faster convergence empirically (Figure 1 left) and theoretically (Figure 1 middle and right). Please refer to the paper for the details. More importantly, we corrected one error in our proof as pointed out by Reviewer 4, and now we prove a convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ under similar assumptions (only difference is we need to assume $\bar{\beta}\le 2\underline{\beta}$, which is satisfied in all our experiments). We admit the convergence analysis is rough, but at least we prove the new algorithm converges in the worst case. We have demonstrated with Figure 1 (new version) that MAdam achieves faster theoretical convergence rate than AMSGrad on the toy problem, and MAdam does converges faster than Adam and LAMB in the large batch experiments.

Regarding the significance of experimental results, we followed a very strict protocol where we search not only the learning rate but also the weight decay and learning rate schedule for the optimizers on each task. A recent work [2] has shown that the test performance of different optimizers are not so huge after careful tuning, especially on easier tasks. Nevertheless, we have shown our methods clearly outperforms the baselines in the toy problems and the large batch training. 

For the baselines, we thought AdaGrad and AdamNC were not popular choices and may not perform as good as Adam on the tasks evaluated, so we did not conduct these experiments. We will try to add these comparisons in our future version. For AMSGrad, we do have comparisons in Sec 4.1 and Appendix D (where MAdam/AMSGrad achieves BLEU scores of 36.07 (0.07)/35.87 (0.05) on IWSLT). For the CIFAR experiments, we use AMSGrad for both Adam and MAdam. AMSGrad was proposed as an "principled exponential moving average variant" instead of an independent optimizer, which store the maximum $v_t$ in $\hat{v}_t$ throughout training and use $\hat{v}_t$  to compute the adaptive learning rate. This is complementary to both MAdam and Adam. The only difference between MAdam and Adam is we use an adaptive $\beta_t$ for $v_t$, so we can also store the maximum $v_t$ in $\hat{v}_t$ and use that to compute the adaptive step size.  As a result, with the CIFAR experiments, we are demonstrating MAdam with AMSGrad outperforms the original AMSGrad (what I would call "Adam with AMSGrad" to distinguish). 

[1] Chen, Xiangyi, Sijia Liu, Ruoyu Sun, and Mingyi Hong. "On the Convergence of A Class of Adam-Type Algorithms for Non-Convex Optimization." ICLR (2019).

[2] Choi, Dami, Christopher J. Shallue, Zachary Nado, Jaehoon Lee, Chris J. Maddison, and George E. Dahl. "On empirical comparisons of optimizers for deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.05446 (2019).

content.title: Review of Adaptive Learning Rates with Maximum Variation Averaging
content.review:
## Summary

In this paper, the authors propose to improve Adam with an iteration dependent averaging weight $\beta_t$. A choice of $\beta_t$ lead to a specific moving average, i.e. a weighting over the past iterations. The authors then compute the variance through time of the gradient $g_t$ with those weights. $\beta_t$ is then chosen greedily so as to maximize the variance at each iteration.

On the theoretical side, the authors provide a weak convergence results (see review hereafter, requires a batch size that goes to infinity, and the bound is in $O(1 / \epsilon^2)$ compared to the best proofs for Adam.

On the practical side, provides experiments on standard vision and NLP datasets, showing that their method is competitive and sometimes better than existing ones.


## Review

The idea of chosing $\beta_t$ in order to maximise the value of the historical variance is appealing. A key intuition is that if a large gradient is seen, it is going to be remembered for a longer time than with the standard Adam. This would make the presented algorithm MAdam somewhere between Adam and AMSGrad.
In fact, if there was no upper bound on $\beta_t$, it is likely a large past gradient would never be forgotten, as assigning more weight to the following smaller iterations would decrease the variance.

The theoretical analysis is quite weak compared to the most recent proofs technique for adaptive methods in the non convex settings [1,2]. In particular, the bound obtained is proportional to $1/\epsilon^2$. Given that $\epsilon$ is typically 1e-8, this makes the bound uninformative. Besides, the analysis requires that the \eta learning rate is smaller than $\epsilon / L$, which is quite impractical, and the batch size to go to infinity, which is not required by standard proofs for Adam or Adagrad.

In fact, with the assumption that $\eta < \epsilon / L$, one can prove the convergence for any choice of v_t in equation (5), as long as it is bounded by G, as the effective learning rate for each coordinate will be between 1/L and 1 / (L + G^2), and the proof quickly boils down to SGD.
This means the authors bypassed most of the difficulties that arise for adaptive methods, in particular the correlation between the numerator and denominator that introduces a bias in the update direction. In Adam or Adagrad, the fact that $\beta_t$ is controlled (Adagrad can be seen as taking $\beta_t = 1-1/t$) means that the correlation is also controlled. With MAdam, this is no longer the case as the effective $\beta_t$ could be as small as 1/2. Large gradients will likely lead to $\beta_t = 1/2$ as this will maximize the observed variance. This will add an uncontrolled bias to the update direction and potentially prevent convergence.
This means that for a specifically crafted example like the one in Reddi et al. 2018 (On the convergence of Adam and Beyond), the method could fail to converge.

Note that it is known that for NLP task, gradients can be normalized (which would be equivalent to taking $\beta_t = 0$), which is done by optimizers like LAMB with good results. Therefore the problem I mentioned in the previous paragraph might not be a problem there. However, it does limit the impact of MAdam as an optimizer for general problems.
The practical results look encouraging even though they are not always significant. 

Because of the strong limitations of the theoretical results in this paper I recommend rejection.

## Remarks

- Section 3, equation (3), (4) and (5): the notation w_t(\beta_t) is weird as w_t also depends on $\beta_{t - 1}$, in particular, $w_t(\beta_t) = \ldots w_{t-1}(\beta_{t-1})$. A more correct notation would be w_t(\beta), or make it depend implicitely on \beta.
- notation with ~ vs no ~ is a bit inconsistent: juse before equation (6), $\tilde{\sigma}$ should maybe be called $\sigma$ as it works with unbiased estimates.
- after eq (7), again confusion between \tilde or no \tilde ("we have abbreviated $u_{t-1}(\beta_{t-1})$ into $\tilde{u}$).
- Theorem 1: instead of taking the batch size going to infinity, one can take $\eta = 1 / \sqrt{T}$ for a known number of time steps T. This gives a $O(1/\sqrt(T))$ rate, which matches the best possible rate for stochastic optimization [3].
- In Section 5.4, the authors say that their methods allow to take a larger learning rate than Adam. This is in fact expected as the maximization of the variance will typically lead to larger values for $v_t$ for MAdam. This can then be compensated by taking a larger $\eta$. However, this does not mean that the effective learning will be larger for MAdam.


[1] A Sufficient Condition for Convergences of Adam and RMSProp, Zou et al. CVPR 2019
[2] On the Convergence of Adam and Adagrad, Defossez et al. arxiv 2020
[3]  Information-theoretic lower bounds on the
oracle complexity of convex optimization, Agarwal et al, Neurips 2007
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: We appreciate your insights of the theoretic analysis!

content.title: We appreciate your insights of the theoretic analysis!
content.comment:
We want to thank you for your analysis, insights, and the papers you have pointed to. We have updated the submission to correct one error in the proof pointed out by Reviewer 4, together with some typos. The convergence rate is now $O(1/\sqrt{T})$. We will also take your suggestion for the notations in our next version, just to avoid introducing new typos in the current version. 

We admit the theoretical results in this paper is weak, but our intention is to provide a justification that it converges. The main goal of this paper is to propose a novel adaptive rule for $\beta_t$, and demonstrate its performance in practice. We show consistent improvements on NLP tasks, and provide fair comparisons for all methods on image classification.  

"With MAdam, this is no longer the case as the effective $\beta_t$ could be as small as 1/2. Large gradients will likely lead to $\beta_t=1/2$ as this will maximize the observed variance. This will add an uncontrolled bias to the update direction and potentially prevent convergence."

In fact, compared with Adam using the same $\alpha$ (or $\beta_1$ as in their paper), we take a smaller step on large gradients, i.e., it is less biased towards directions with large gradients. Recall our update rules in Algorithm 1. Note $\tilde{m}_t$ and $\tilde{v}_t$ are computed using a constant $\alpha$ and a variable $\beta_t$ respectively. Therefore, when $g_t$ is large and $\beta_t$ is small, we will obtain a larger $\tilde{v}_t$ and thus smaller adaptive step size (ignoring the effect of $w_t$, which usually converges to 1 quickly) compared with Adam. Also note we do use gradient normalization in the large batch experiments, same as LAMB. But we do not use that for other experiments.


"In fact, with the assumption that $\eta < \eta/L$, one can prove the convergence for any choice of v_t in equation (5), as long as it is bounded by G, as the effective learning rate for each coordinate will be between 1/L and 1 / (L + G^2), and the proof quickly boils down to SGD."

Thank you for the brilliant idea! This does seem to simplify the proof a lot, especially for the second-order term in Eq. 17. However, for MAdam, $\beta_t$ is correlated with $g_t$. Therefore, we will face the same issue as Lemma 2 (in current version) addresses when bounding its first-order term. This results in an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate in the current version.

Regarding your suggestion about setting $\eta=1/\sqrt{T}$ instead of using an increasing batch size: unfortunately, in our current proof, this cannot effectively reduce the gradient noise to 0. There will be a constant gradient noise term in the upper bound if we do not adopt the increasing batch size assumption. In fact, this batch size assumption holds well in the large-batch experiments, where we use a batch size no lower than 32K and a total of only 2075 iterations.

content.title: the novelty is not enough
content.review:
In this paper, the authors presented an algorithm based on ADAM, which modified the choice of exponential decay rate as well as the batch size. The main issue is the lack of novelty. In my point of view, the convergence analysis has little difference with [1], unless a better convergence rate is achieved. Actually, the convergence rate is worse than SGD.

I think many researchers do not even notice the issue in [2], the fist & second moments are not unbiased since limit and expectation are not able to switch unless be proved. As a result, I can hardly agree with the statement “Then, the unbiased local estimate of the gradient variance…” in Sec.3( page 3). 

The third issue is the O(T) increasement of sample size. Practically, what if T greater than or equal to the training data size?  I think we are not able to construct a convergent sequence.

There are many typos in the paper, e.g. $\mathrm{E}_t [g_t] = f(\theta_t)$ in page 12.

In conclusion, I think the contribution is not enough to make the paper be accepted. 

[1] Manzil Zaheer, Sashank Reddi, Devendra Sachan, Satyen Kale, and Sanjiv Kumar. Adaptive methods for nonconvex optimization. In NeurIPS, pp. 9793–9803, 2018.
[2] Diederik P. Kingma and Jimmy Ba. Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. In Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun (eds.), ICLR, 2015. URL http://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980.

replying_to: Replying to the novelty is not enough

content.title: You missed the novelty
content.comment:
Thank you for the careful review and identifying the typos in the paper. We have revised the paper, correcting an error in the proof pointed out by Reviewer 4, and moved one synthetic experiment into the main paper (Sec. 4.1) to provide a refined analysis comparing MAdam and AMSGrad. 

We think our main novelty is to propose the adaptive $\beta_t$ that works well in practice, but you never mentioned in your review why this is not something novel to you. Our focus is not on proposing a novel theoretical analysis showing ground-breaking improvements of previous analysis, but to show it converges in the worst case. The majority of the papers on adaptive optimizers do not have such ground-breaking theoretical analysis showing faster convergence than SGD.

We also agree the usage of "unbiased" is misleading and have changed that into "biase-corrected". In fact, the word "unbiased" never appears in the current version of the Adam paper. Dividing by $w_t$ corrects the moment estimators from biasing towards 0, not necessarily making them closer to the expectation, which is also the point of the Adam paper. We do not see the "limit" in Eq. 2 of Adam or our paper, therefore do not quite understand your comment about "the fist & second moments are not unbiased since limit and expectation are not able to switch unless be proved".

The O(T) increase in sample size is an assumption in the theorem, not a component of our algorithm. However, this assumption holds in our large batch experiments, where we use a batch size of 32K and a total of 2075 iterations (so T is upper bounded by batch size). Note the same assumption is adopted by, e.g., SignSGD.
